hero.title: Null-safety
intro.0: Sooner or later a value is not there - a name nobody filled in, an object that was never built. Ask an absent value to do something and the program crashes. The fix is to plan for the empty case: hand back a default, skip safely, or say plainly that you do not know. You write each move and run it.
task.1.title: Fall back when there is nothing
task.1.context:
Sometimes a value is simply **absent** - a name nobody filled in, a lookup that found nothing. In C# an absent value is `null`. Ask for its length and the program crashes.

The safe move is to supply a fallback: *use this value, or that default when there is nothing*. C# writes it with `??` - `given ?? "stray"` means "`given`, unless it is `null`, in which case `"stray"`".

Write a `Shelter` whose `NameOr(string? given)` returns the name it is handed, or `"stray"` when that name is `null`.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Shelter` a `string NameOr(string? given)` that returns `given`, or `"stray"` when `given` is `null`.
task.2.title: Reach through something that might be missing
task.2.context:
It is not only plain values that go missing - a whole **object** can be absent. If `pet` is `null`, then `pet.Name` crashes: you cannot ask a nothing for its name.

Many languages give you a *safe* way to reach through: if the thing is there, follow the dot; if it is `null`, stop and hand back `null` instead of crashing. C# writes this with `?.` - `pet?.Name` is the pet's name when there is a pet, and `null` when there is not.

Write a `Tag` whose `Greet(Pet? pet)` returns the pet's `Name`, or `"nobody"` when the pet itself is `null`.
task.2.goal.0: Give `Tag` a `string Greet(Pet? pet)` that returns `pet?.Name`, falling back to `"nobody"` when `pet` is `null`.
task.3.title: A number that might not be there
task.3.context:
A plain `int` always holds some number - there is no room in it for "no value". But sometimes you genuinely do not have one yet: an age nobody entered, a score not recorded.

C# lets a value type opt in to being absent by adding `?`: an `int?` is either a real number or `null`. Before you use the number, you check: is there one? Ask `age == null` (or `age.HasValue`), and reach for the number with `age.Value` only once you know it is there.

Write a `Vet` whose `Describe(int? age)` returns `"unknown"` when the age is `null`, and otherwise `"age "` followed by the number.
task.3.goal.0: Give `Vet` a `string Describe(int? age)` that returns `"unknown"` when `age` is `null`.
task.3.goal.1: Otherwise return `"age "` joined with the number, so `Describe(4)` reads `age 4`.
task.4.title: Set a default only when it is empty
task.4.context:
A common need: fill a slot with a default, but only if nothing is there yet - never overwrite a value someone already gave.

You could write it the long way (`if (occupant == null) occupant = "guest";`). C# has a shorthand that does exactly that: `??=` assigns the right-hand value **only when the left side is `null`**. `occupant ??= "guest"` leaves a real occupant untouched and fills in `"guest"` when the slot is empty.

Write a `Kennel` with a `string? occupant` field and a `CheckIn(string? given)` that stores `given`, defaults it to `"guest"` when `given` is `null`, and returns the occupant.
task.4.goal.0: Give `Kennel` a `string? occupant` field and a `string CheckIn(string? given)` method.
task.4.goal.1: Store `given` in `occupant`, then use `??=` to default it to `"guest"` when it is `null`, and return it.
task.5.title: What you learned
task.5.context: Four ways to meet a value that might not be there - so a missing value bends your program instead of breaking it.
task.5.summaryIntro: Every language has a way to say "there is nothing here" - C# calls it `null`. The danger is not the absence itself; it is code that assumes a value is always present. You handled the absent case four ways:
task.5.summaryItems.0.title: Fall back with `??` -
task.5.summaryItems.0.text: `given ?? "stray"` uses the value when there is one and a default when it is `null`.
task.5.summaryItems.1.title: Reach through safely with `?.` -
task.5.summaryItems.1.text: `pet?.Name` follows the dot when the object is there and stops at `null` instead of crashing.
task.5.summaryItems.2.title: Let a number be absent with `int?` -
task.5.summaryItems.2.text: an `int?` is either a real number or `null`; check first, then read `.Value`.
task.5.summaryItems.3.title: Default only when empty with `??=` -
task.5.summaryItems.3.text: `occupant ??= "guest"` fills the slot only when it is `null`, never overwriting a real value.
task.5.summaryClose: The portable habit outlasts the operators: wherever a value can be absent, decide what absent means here - a default, a safe skip, or a clear "unknown" - rather than letting it crash. Other languages spell it `null`, `nil`, `None`, or an optional; the thinking is the same.
concept.pr-null-coalescing.def: Supplying a fallback for an absent value with ?? (and filling a slot only when empty with ??=).
concept.pr-null-conditional.def: Reaching through an object that might be missing with ?., which stops at null instead of crashing.
concept.pr-nullable-value-type.def: A plain value like int or bool that opts in to being absent by adding ?, like int?, so it is either the value or null.
